Title: A Transcontinental Railroad
Author: by Mark Clemens
Content: The idea of a transcontinental¹ railroad came into being when California and the western territories were beginning to be settled by large groups of people. A group of businessmen predicted that a railroad which connected the east coast with the west would make a good deal of money in trade. They even expected to transport goods brought to California from China.

At first, the building of a transcontinental railroad seemed an impossible task. In 1862, President Lincoln signed a bill which gave the railroad companies special land grants and government bonds to help pay for the job. Even so, the owners of the companies had to find ways to raise more money.

The Central Pacific Railroad began construction in Sacramento, California in 1863. The Union Pacific began in Omaha, Nebraska in December of the same year. In less than four years, 1,776 miles of track were laid across a wilderness.

Both companies had tremendous difficulty getting their supplies. The Central Pacific had to ship their equipment from the Atlantic coast. The only way to do this was to send it either across the Isthmus of Panama² or around Cape Horn³ to San Francisco. This was very expensive, and took a long time.

The Union Pacific had their own problems. At first, they had to ship their supplies and equipment up the Missouri River by steamboat, then carry them overland by stagecoach and in wagons. Later, they were able to send supplies along the tracks they had laid, but this was slow, and hardly an improvement. All the digging and carrying, pushing and pulling had to be done by men with picks and shovels, wheelbarrows, wagons and mules. It took the labor of hundreds of men . . . to complete this incredible task. Work continued for many years after 1869. Even though the tracks were laid, there was still work to be done grading⁴ and banking⁵ along the way.

Ten years after the Golden Spike Ceremony⁶, Robert Louis Stevenson traveled across America by train. You can read in the descriptions entered in his journal that trains were still far from comfortable. But over the years, they did improve. For a time, they were a popular way to travel and an inexpensive way to ship things.

Railroad companies began losing money when the automobile and the truck were developed. Many companies were forced out of business. Today, it is just as common to see an abandoned railroad track as it is to see a used one. But the story of railroads does not end here. Perhaps . . . we can look forward to using the rails again, and the development of a new and improved technology.

References: transcontinental: going across a continent—in this case, North America
Isthmus of Panama: a narrow strip of land connecting North and South America
Cape Horn: the southernmost tip of South America
grading: giving a surface a slope
banking: building a railway curve with the outer rail higher than the inner rail
Golden Spike Ceremony: ceremony celebrating the completion of the transcontinental railroad held in Promontory Point, Utah
